speaker: Peter Beck
title: How Rocket Lab CEO Sir Peter Beck Is Building a Multi-Generational Space Company
question: In commercial spaceflight, why do small launch vehicle manufacturers often end up building their own dedicated launch sites instead of using major existing ranges?
guest: At the end of the day, if you have a small launch vehicle and you turn up to a large launchpad, the reality is that the fees do not change. When you are trying to sell a rocket for $8 million, you cannot have a million and a half dollars worth of launch fees. On a $50 million rocket, it does not make any difference. So we realized very early on that in order for this to be financially viable, we needed our own launch site. Ultimately we felt it was easier to do that in New Zealand. New Zealand had no space industry, so sometimes it is easier to start something from scratch and formulate it in a way that best makes sense than to try and integrate with a whole bunch of rules that do not fit.

points.core: Fixed range fees at large launchpads do not scale down for small rockets.
points.note: Accept: shared government or heavy-lift launchpad fees remaining largely invariant regardless of rocket size. Do not credit: generic statements that launchpads are expensive or crowded.

points.core: Flat launch fees consume a crippling share of a small rocket's price.
points.note: Accept: million-dollar-plus range costs breaking unit economics on sub-$10M rockets while staying minor on $50M+ heavy vehicles. Do not credit: vague references to high overhead without contrasting small versus large vehicle economics.

points.core: Greenfield jurisdictions allow designing fit-for-purpose launch regulations from scratch.
points.note: Accept: operating where no legacy space regulatory regime exists to avoid retrofitting mismatched incumbent rules. Do not credit: generic claims about deregulation or lower taxes.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Small launch companies build their own sites mainly because their business model depends on frequent, responsive, low-cost launches, and the big government-run ranges are poorly suited to that.

At major ranges such as Cape Canaveral or Vandenberg, a small launcher is a low-priority tenant. It must fit its schedule around national security, NASA, and large commercial missions, share range safety and tracking assets, and accept delays when a higher-priority launch slips. Range fees, security requirements, and bureaucratic overhead were designed around large rockets and can be disproportionate for a vehicle whose launch price is only a few million dollars.

A private site gives the company control over its own schedule, infrastructure, and operations, with pads and integration facilities tailored to its vehicle rather than adapted from someone else's. It can also be located for clear downrange corridors and access to the desired orbits, especially the sun-synchronous and polar orbits popular with small satellites, with little air and sea traffic to clear.

Rocket Lab is the classic example: its privately owned complex on New Zealand's Mahia Peninsula is licensed for very frequent launches, something it could not have obtained at a busy US federal range.

points.why: The candidate says range fees were designed around large rockets but never establishes that those fees stay roughly the same for smaller rockets.

The candidate describes a potentially disproportionate burden from fees and overhead without explaining how the same fee can undermine a small launcher's economics while remaining minor for a large launcher.
The New Zealand example highlights frequent-launch licensing without connecting it to the opportunity to design launch regulations from scratch.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Small launch vehicle manufacturers build dedicated launch sites primarily to control their schedules, contain per-launch costs, and streamline operations. Major existing ranges like Cape Canaveral and Vandenberg suffer from heavy congestion and prioritize national security missions and large, high-cadence rockets, frequently bumping smaller operators and restricting available launch windows. Because small launchers compete against cheap rideshare missions by promising responsive, tailored delivery to specific orbits on a customer’s timetable, unpredictable range delays directly undermine their core value proposition.

Major government ranges also impose steep fixed support fees, legacy tracking requirements, and complex multi-agency bureaucracy designed around heavy-lift vehicles, creating disproportionate overhead for low-margin small rockets. By building private or dedicated pads—such as Rocket Lab’s Launch Complex 1 in New Zealand—manufacturers can design lean, automated ground infrastructure matched to their specific rocket, conduct rapid testing without disrupting neighboring pads, and utilize uncongested airspace and maritime corridors. Ultimately, developing a dedicated site trades upfront capital investment for operational autonomy, rapid turnaround, and the schedule certainty that small-satellite customers pay a premium to secure.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Small launch companies mostly build their own pads because the big government ranges don't fit how they need to operate. The main draw of a small rocket is frequent, responsive launches on the customer's schedule. At busy ranges like Cape Canaveral or Vandenberg, they have to queue behind government, crewed and heavy-lift missions, and they share range assets, safety crews and airspace closures. That causes delays and scheduling conflicts they can't control. Range fees, pad leases and required infrastructure are also sized for large vehicles, so on a small rocket's thin margins those costs eat up a big share of each launch's revenue.

A private site lets the company design the pad around its own vehicle, iterate quickly, and launch as often as its business needs. Small rockets have smaller hazard areas, so remote sites become possible. Those can offer clear flight paths over open ocean to desirable orbits, such as sun-synchronous or a wide range of inclinations, with few airspace or shipping conflicts. Rocket Lab's Mahia site in New Zealand, licensed for launches as often as every 72 hours, is the classic example. Local governments and spaceport authorities often add subsidies or easier permitting, which strengthens the case for a dedicated site.

points.why: The candidate describes range costs as sized for large vehicles but never establishes that the fees stay the same for smaller rockets.
The candidate says range costs consume a large share of a small launch’s revenue but does not contrast that burden with the smaller share those same fees consume on a large launch.
The candidate mentions easier permitting in general but does not explain how the absence of legacy space regulations lets a jurisdiction design rules suited to small launch operations.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Small launch vehicle manufacturers often build their own launch sites because major government-run ranges are poorly suited to their business model, which relies on rapid turnaround, flexible scheduling, and low per-launch costs. Legacy ranges like Cape Canaveral and Vandenberg prioritize large national security and heavy-lift commercial missions, meaning small-rocket operators frequently face long queues, rigid scheduling windows, and costly delays whenever higher-priority launches take precedence. These established facilities also impose substantial range fees, complex administrative overhead, and safety protocols scaled for massive vehicles, which can quickly erode the tight margins of a small launcher. By operating a dedicated private site—often in a remote coastal location with minimal air and maritime traffic—manufacturers gain full control over their launch cadence and can tailor simple, lightweight pad infrastructure specifically to their vehicle. Remote private sites can also provide wide, unobstructed over-water launch azimuths that make it easier to reach diverse polar and sun-synchronous orbits on demand.

Small launch vehicle manufacturers often build dedicated pads because their business depends on launching on short notice at a price that makes sense for small payloads. At a busy range, even a company with its own pad may have to schedule around other launches, military operations, and shared tracking and safety resources. Range fees and the cost of adapting an existing pad to the vehicle can also eat into the margins on a small launch.

A dedicated site lets the company tailor the pad and ground equipment to its rocket, schedule more of its own operations, and choose a location with safe flight paths to the orbits its customers need. Building and operating a site is expensive, so the trade-off makes the most sense when the company expects enough launches to spread those fixed costs.

The response discusses tailoring facilities and selecting flight paths but omits the ability to design launch regulations from scratch in a jurisdiction without legacy space rules.

A small launcher can offer customers a flight to a specific orbit on a date they choose. At a busy range, though, it may have to wait for a launch window, tracking crews, or safety clearance while larger government and commercial missions take priority. Even when the range has an opening, its pads may need costly modifications to handle the vehicle’s propellants and ground equipment.

A dedicated site lets the manufacturer build only the infrastructure its rocket needs and choose a location with a safe flight path to the orbits its customers want. The company takes on the cost of building and operating the site, but gains more control over when and how often it can launch.
